 Allegheny County bill on property tax rights advances to full council
 MEGAN TROTTER 
 TribLive
 Mon, Nov 9, 2026 • 07:06 PM 
 Share

 A sign above the office where residents can pay Allegheny County taxes in-person, inside the Allegheny County Courthouse in Downtown Pittsburgh on Friday, June 14, 2024. (Justin Vellucci | TribLive)
 Allegheny County Council’s government reform committee advanced legislation on Monday that would establish permanent standards for real estate billing, including deadlines for mailing bills and extensions for taxpayers when bills are delayed.
 The proposal seeks to make existing billing reforms permanent under future treasurers , ensuring taxpayers receive clear information about property assessments, tax rates, total amounts owed, payment deadlines, discounts and penalties. It was sponsored by Allegheny County Councilman Dan Grzybek and developed with the Allegheny County Treasurer’s Office.
 “Our office strongly supports the taxpayer bill of rights. We’ve worked collaboratively on this legislation because we share the same goal: making government more efficient, transparent and responsive to the taxpayers,” said County Treasurer Erica Rocchi Brusselars.
 The legislation, referred to as a Tax Bill Disclosure Bill of Rights, was advanced unanimously by the committee to the full 15-member council.
 If passed, the legislation would protect taxpayers from losing the 2% early-payment discount when the county fails to issue tax bills on time. Discount deadlines would be extended by 60 days if an individual’s bill is not available by Jan. 31.
 The measure would require the treasurer to notify the county executive, county council president and the public within two business days of missing the deadline, in addition to providing an estimated date for when the bills will become available.
 The 60 days would begin after the bill becomes available, while the full-payment deadline would extend to 90 days.
 The ordinance would also allow taxpayers to request written payment of receipts.
 “Seems like some very common sense reforms here. Excellent to hear about them and excited to codify them,” said Councilman Alex Rose, I-Squirrel Hill. “I think this is an excellent way for different branches of government to collaborate and ensure good governance in the future.”
 The Tax Bill Disclosure Bill of Rights will need a supporting vote from at least eight members of the full council to pass.
